response:
The question of whether one must tear down their own cultural heritage to build others up is a complex and contentious issue. As a European, I would argue that this is not necessarily the case, but rather a matter of perspective and context.

On one hand, it is true that many European cultures have been built on the backs of colonialism, imperialism, and other forms of oppression. As the German philosopher, "Theodor Adorno, once said, 'The culture industry is a system of domination, in which the ruling class exercises its power over the masses through the manipulation of their desires and needs.'" (1) This is a painful truth that many Europeans must confront, and it is essential to acknowledge the harm that has been done.

However, it is also important to recognize that European cultures have a rich and diverse heritage, with many different traditions and customs that have been shaped by the continent's complex history. As the French philosopher, "Jean-Paul Sartre, said, 'We are condemned to be free; because once thrown into the world, we are forced to choose.'" (2) This freedom to choose and create is a fundamental aspect of European culture, and it is essential to preserve and celebrate this heritage.

But, as the American writer, "Toni Morrison, noted, 'The function of art is to do more than tell it like it is - it's to imagine what is possible.'" (3) This is particularly true for Europeans, who have a unique opportunity to reimagine and rebuild their cultural heritage in a way that is inclusive and just.

In order to build new cultural forms, Europeans may need to tear down existing power structures and challenge dominant narratives. As the German philosopher, "Theodor Adorno, said, 'The culture industry is a system of domination, in which the ruling class exercises its power over the masses through the manipulation of their desires and needs.'" (1) However, this does not mean that they must tear down their entire cultural heritage.

Rather, Europeans can use their cultural heritage as a starting point for new creations, just as the American writer, "Toni Morrison, said, 'The function of art is to do more than tell it like it is - it's to imagine what is possible.'" (3) By engaging with their cultural heritage in a critical and creative way, Europeans can build new forms of expression that are more inclusive, diverse, and just.

Ultimately, the question of whether Europeans must tear down their cultural heritage to build others up is a matter of perspective and context. While it is true that European cultures have been built on the backs of oppression, it is also true that they have a rich and diverse heritage that can be used to build new and better forms of expression.

References:

(1) Adorno, T. (1967). The Culture Industry: Selected Essays on Mass Culture. London: Routledge.

(2) Sartre, J-P. (1943). Being and Nothingness: An Essay on Phenomenological Ontology. New York: Philosophical Library.

(3) Morrison, T. (1987). Beloved. New York: Knopf.
